ns1:channel.ns1:title: Nature Medicine
ns1:channel.ns1:description: Original research articles published in Nature Medicine range from basic findings that have clear implications for disease pathogenesis and therapy to the earliest phases of human investigation. Aiming to keep Ph.D. and M.D. readers informed of a wide range of biomedical research findings, the journal publishes the latest advances in cancer biology, vascular biology, neuroscience, inflammatory disease, infectious disease and metabolic disorders, among other fields. Reviews, Perspectives and other commissioned content clarify and give context to these biomedical research advances, and the News section reports on the latest developments in drug research and development.

ns1:item.ns1:title: Optogenetic therapy shows early promise for treating retinitis pigmentosa
ns1:item.ns5:encoded:
Nature Medicine, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41591-026-00051-1

In a small study involving patients with blindness due to advanced retinitis pigmentosa, optogenetic therapy appears safe; early efficacy signals are promising and reveal opportunities for technical refinement.
ns1:item.dc:title: Optogenetic therapy shows early promise for treating retinitis pigmentosa
ns1:item.dc:creator: Karen O’Leary

ns1:item.ns1:title: Hidden race disparities in cancer treatment toxicity
ns1:item.ns5:encoded:
Nature Medicine, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41591-026-00050-2

Large-scale analysis of real-world data reveals racial disparities in the occurrence of immune-related adverse events during cancer immunotherapy — which were not evident in trial data, owing to the enrollment of mostly white patients.
ns1:item.dc:title: Hidden race disparities in cancer treatment toxicity
ns1:item.dc:creator: Karen O’Leary

ns1:item.ns1:title: Making AI work in healthcare
ns1:item.ns5:encoded:
Nature Medicine, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04726-7

Drawing on experiences across diverse settings, this issue of Nature Medicine explores the challenges of and lessons learned from the deployment of artificial intelligence models into healthcare.

ns1:item.ns1:title: Personalized neoantigen-targeting cancer vaccines in ovarian cancer: a phase 1 trial
ns1:item.ns5:encoded:
Nature Medicine, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04717-8

A phase 1 trial shows that treatment of patients with high-grade serous ovarian cancer with personalized neoantigen vaccines combined with PD-1 blockade was feasible and led to tumor-specific immune responses in many patients and putative mechanisms of resistance related to antigen presentation were identified via cell-free DNA analysis.
ns1:item.dc:title: Personalized neoantigen-targeting cancer vaccines in ovarian cancer: a phase 1 trial

ns1:item.ns1:title: Talazoparib plus enzalutamide in high-volume metastatic hormone-naive prostate cancer: a randomized phase 2 trial
ns1:item.ns5:encoded:
Nature Medicine, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04671-5

In the randomized multicenter phase 2 ZZ-FIRST trial, patients with high-volume metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer treated with poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor talazoparib combined with androgen receptor inhibitor enzalutamide had an improved prostate-specific antigen response compared with enzalutamide alone, and spatial transcriptomic analyses of paired biopsies linked AR inhibition-induced suppression of HRR-related programs to proliferation arrest rather than functional HRR deficiency.
ns1:item.dc:title: Talazoparib plus enzalutamide in high-volume metastatic hormone-naive prostate cancer: a randomized phase 2 trial

ns1:item.ns1:title: Characterizing the onset and progression of cancer cachexia using routine clinical data
ns1:item.ns5:encoded:
Nature Medicine, Published online: 13 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04720-z

In 52,236 patients with cancer, cachectic weight loss episodes were linked to lower survival rates, occurred at times of disease progression, and carried a consistent serological signature across routine laboratory markers. Specific tumor genotypes, including TP53 mutations, were also positively associated with cachexia risk. Statistical models were trained to predict a patient’s impending risk of cachexia.
ns1:item.dc:title: Characterizing the onset and progression of cancer cachexia using routine clinical data

ns1:item.ns1:title: Autologous and broadly neutralizing antibodies drive ART-free HIV control
ns1:item.ns5:encoded:
Nature Medicine, Published online: 13 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04714-x

A secondary analysis of trial data shows that both host antibodies and infused antibodies against HIV help to delay viral rebound after interruption of antiretroviral therapy (ART), which could inform approaches to durable, ART-free HIV control.
ns1:item.dc:title: Autologous and broadly neutralizing antibodies drive ART-free HIV control
ns1:item.dc:creator: Worapong Nasomsong
Jonathan Z. Li
